b: GMs Nodirbek Abdusattorov and Andy Woodward started with wins in round one of the XTX Markets London Chess Classic 2026 on Wednesday. Defending Champion Abdusattorov (with White) defeated GM Shreyas Royal in a Benoni pawn structure with reversed colors, while Woodward had the black pieces in a Sicilian duel with GM Ihor Samunenkov.
Round two is on Thursday, November 26, starting at 11 a.m. ET / 17:00 CET / 9:30 p.m. IST.
Abdusattorov and Woodward are in the lead, but there are eight rounds to go.
All the other games ended in draws—not without missed chances!—as you can see in the results graphic below.

The London Chess Classic, first held in 2009, is back for its fourth edition since 2020. COVID-19 caused a three-year interruption, but since 2023 the UK's most prestigious invitational tournament has been an annual recurrence.

Abdusattorov won last year's edition by a remarkable two-point margin over GM Alireza Firouzja, and he's back this year to defend his title. The star-studded field includes English legends and youngsters alike, as well as multi-generational talents from abroad. On the English side are the legendary GMs Michael Adams (55), Luke McShane (42), and Gawain Maroroa Jones (38) to represent the "older guard," with 17-year-old Royal stepping in for Generation Z.

On the international side, American GMs Levon Aronian (44) and Woodward (16) are 27 years and six months apart, and Ukrainian GMs Vasyl Ivanchuk (57) and Samunenkov (17) have 40 years between them. GM Nihal Sarin (22) is from India, and Abdusattorov (also 22) is from Uzbekistan.
This year's event takes place at the London Novotel West in Hammersmith, London, England. But the opening ceremony took place at the iconic Tower of London.

It's a single round-robin with 10 players and a time control of 90 minutes for 40 moves plus 30 minutes after move 40, with a 30-second increment starting on move one.

The first game to end was the encounter of Ivanchuk vs. Nihal, and the Ukrainian grandmaster had some chances to win with an extra pawn. He was "pretty happy" with his opening preparation, he said, and the players followed a GM Magnus Carlsen game from 2006 for the first 19 moves. Nihal played a defensive pawn sacrifice with 21...d5?!, and although Nihal's concept worked, Ivanchuk did have his chances.

In a shrug-your-shoulders tone, Ivanchuk seemed unsatisfied with the draw but gave credit to his opponent. "Okay, hard to be happy because I was clearly better out of the opening, but okay, my opponent defended well," he said.

We saw two more draws in Aronian vs. McShane and Jones vs. Adams. Aronian achieved what might be called a symbolic advantage with White in the Four Knights Spanish; he had a better pawn structure, but no concrete way to make use of that. Adams, on the other hand, had a serious chance to win with Black, but ultimately drew with a pawn for the exchange.
As often happens, the last mistake occurred exactly on move 40, when Adams had just three minutes left before receiving another half hour.

Abdusattorov's win was praised as the game of the day by the commentators, and indeed it looked like a one-sided bulldozing. The game started as an English Opening, but by move 15 very clearly took on the contours of a Benoni Defense with reversed colors. Abdusattorov's energetic 21.c5? looked great in the game, and it worked out, even if the computer finds some incredible resources for the black pieces. As it happened, the initiative swept Royal off his feet.

Woodward won his game before Abdusattorov, and this one came from the black side of the Moscow Variation in the Sicilian Defense. Woodward played the combative response 3...Nd7, and by move 12 the position looked like it came out of a Sicilian Najdorf. As is quite typical in the Sicilian Defense—when it goes well for Black—he mounted great pressure down the half-open c-file.
The Challengers group, taking place alongside the Masters, is hardly less exciting and features a world-class field.
GM Mateusz Bartel, GM Rasmus Svane, and IM Carissa Yip lead after the first round.
With the world championship ongoing as well, we will cover this event again after rounds five and nine. Enjoy the show!

The London Chess Classic takes place on November 25-December 4 at the London Novotel West in Hammersmith, London, England. Defending champion GM Nodirbek Abdusattorov leads a star-studded 10-player field in the Masters tournament, one of England's strongest and most traditional invitational tournaments. It is a single round-robin with a time control of 90 minutes for 40 moves followed by 30 minutes for the rest of the game, plus a 30-second increment starting on move one.
